title: Magnetism
summary: Magnets, the magnetic field of a current, and forces in a field.
cards.0.p: A magnet attracts materials such as iron. A magnet has two poles, N and S. The N end of a hanging magnet turns north. Like poles repel each other, and opposite poles attract.
cards.0.svg#10: red: N pole · blue: S pole
cards.0.key: Attraction does not prove that an object is a magnet, because iron is attracted too. Repulsion proves it.
cards.1.h: A single pole cannot be isolated
cards.1.p: Every piece of a broken magnet still has two poles. Magnetism comes from the tiny magnets in atoms lining up in the same direction. That is why an N or S pole is never found on its own.
cards.1.svg#14: each piece is again a magnet with N and S poles
cards.1.key: In a magnet that is heated or struck, this alignment is disturbed and the magnetism weakens.
cards.2.p: The region where a magnet has an effect is called a magnetic field. The field is shown with B, and its unit is the tesla. Field lines are closed curves and run from N to S outside the magnet. Where the lines are dense, the field is strong.
cards.2.svg#3: closed curves · dense lines = strong field
cards.2.key: The N end of a compass needle shows the direction of the field. Inside the magnet the lines run from S to N, and they never cross.
cards.3.h: Earth's magnetic field and the compass
cards.3.p: Earth is like a giant magnet. Since the N end of a compass points north, there is a magnetic S pole near geographic north. These poles do not coincide exactly, and the angle between them is called the declination.
cards.3.key: The magnetic poles slowly move. That is why the declination changes over the years.
cards.3.once.soru: The N end of a compass points north. Which magnetic pole is at Earth's geographic north?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: The N end of the needle is attracted by the opposite pole. So there is a magnetic S pole at geographic north.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: Like poles repel each other. If there were an N pole there, the N end of the needle would turn south.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: Earth behaves like a giant magnet and has two poles.
cards.4.p: Earth's magnetic field is also tilted toward the ground. The angle that a needle turning in a vertical plane makes with the horizontal is called the inclination. This angle is 0° at the magnetic equator and 90° at the poles.
cards.4.key: Declination is measured in the horizontal plane, and inclination in the vertical plane. The inclination is 0° near the equator and 90° at the magnetic poles.
cards.4.svg#7: 0° at the magnetic equator, 90° at the magnetic poles
cards.4.once.soru: At the north magnetic pole, how does the N end of a compass needle that can turn in a vertical plane sit?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: At the north magnetic pole the field lines enter the ground vertically, and the inclination is 90°. At the south magnetic pole, the N end of the needle points straight up.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: The needle sits horizontal at the magnetic equator.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: That happens somewhere between the equator and the pole.
cards.5.p: Materials that are strongly attracted to a magnet and can be magnetized are called ferromagnetic. Iron, nickel, and cobalt are among them. Aluminum is attracted very weakly, and copper is repelled very weakly.
cards.5.svg#12: can become a permanent magnet: ferromagnetic
cards.5.key: Aluminum is a paramagnetic material. Copper, bismuth, and water are diamagnetic. Permanent magnets are made only from ferromagnetic materials.
cards.5.etk.soru: A ferromagnetic material is strongly attracted, a paramagnetic one weakly attracted, and a diamagnetic one weakly repelled. Which is this material?
cards.5.etk.ogeler.5.2: Copper is diamagnetic. It does not stick to a magnet.
cards.5.etk.ogeler.6.2: Bismuth is one of the strongest diamagnetic materials.
cards.5.once.soru: You bring a magnet close to a copper wire. What happens?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: Copper is repelled very weakly, and this effect cannot be seen by eye.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: The strongly attracted ones are iron, nickel, and cobalt.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: The repulsion of copper is very weak.
cards.6.h: Field of a straight current-carrying wire
cards.6.p: A wire carrying current creates a circular field around itself. In the right-hand rule, the thumb shows the direction of the current and the curled fingers show the direction of the field. The field is found with B = 2k·I/d.
cards.6.key: The symbol ⊗ shows a current going into the page, and ⊙ a current coming out of the page. k = 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. If the distance doubles, the field is halved.
cards.7.p: A solenoid (coil) behaves like a bar magnet. The field inside it is uniform and is found with B = 4πk·N·I/L. When the four fingers curl in the direction of the current, the thumb shows the N pole.
cards.7.key: Here N is the number of turns and L is the length of the solenoid. The field at the center of a single loop is B = 2πk·I/r.
cards.7.once.soru: You double the number of turns of a coil. The current and length are the same. What happens to the field inside?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: Every turn contributes to the field. So the field is directly proportional to the number of turns.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: The field gets stronger as the turns increase.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: The field depends on the number of turns.
cards.8.p: When a soft iron core is placed inside the solenoid, the field becomes many times stronger. This is called an electromagnet. When the current is cut, the magnetism disappears. The strength of an electromagnet increases with the number of turns and the current.
cards.8.key: An electromagnet is used in scrap cranes, bells, relays, and door locks. You can switch it on and off and adjust its strength with the current. That is its advantage.
cards.9.h: Force on a wire in a field
cards.9.p: A force acts on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field: F = B·I·L·sinθ. If the wire is parallel to the field the force is zero, and if it is perpendicular the force is greatest. In the right-hand rule, the four fingers show B, the thumb shows I, and the palm shows F.
cards.9.svg#3: B into the page (⊗) · I ⊥ B → F is greatest
cards.9.key: A loudspeaker works this way too. A changing current is fed to a coil in the field of a magnet. This current creates a changing force and makes the cone vibrate.
cards.10.p: If two parallel wires carry currents in the same direction, the wires attract each other. If they carry currents in opposite directions, they repel each other. The two forces are equal: F/L = 2k·I₁·I₂/d.
cards.10.key: Currents in the same direction attract each other. Do not confuse this with the rule in electricity that 'like charges repel each other'.
cards.10.once.soru: Two wires side by side carry currents in the same direction. What do the wires do?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: Each wire feels a force in the field of the other. Currents in the same direction attract each other.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: Every wire carrying current creates a field. The other wire feels a force in this field.
cards.11.p: A magnetic field exerts a force only on a moving charge: F = q·v·B·sinθ. No force acts on a charge that is at rest or moving parallel to the field. An electron is pushed in the opposite direction.
cards.11.key: If v = 0 or v ∥ B, then F = 0. For a positive charge, the direction of the force is found as it is for a current.
cards.11.once.soru: You place an electron at rest next to a magnet. Does a magnetic force act on it?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: The magnetic force acts only on a moving charge. If v = 0, then F = 0.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: A magnetic field does not attract a charge at rest.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: A magnetic field does not repel a charge at rest.
cards.12.h: A charge entering perpendicular to the field moves in a circle
cards.12.p: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity and changes only the direction of the velocity. So the charge moves in a circle: r = m·v/(q·B). This force does no work, and the kinetic energy does not change.
cards.12.svg#4: F ⊥ v → no work, constant speed
cards.12.key: q·v·B = m·v²/r. If the speed doubles, r doubles too. The period T = 2πm/(q·B), however, does not change.
cards.12.once.soru: What happens over time to the speed of a charge that enters perpendicular to the field?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: The force is perpendicular to the velocity. It changes only the direction and does not make the speed larger or smaller.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: A force perpendicular to the velocity does no work. So the kinetic energy does not increase.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: A force perpendicular to the velocity does not slow the charge down.
cards.13.p: Opposite forces act on the opposite sides of a current-carrying loop between magnets, and the loop turns. The commutator reverses the current every half turn. A motor converts electricity into motion.
cards.13.svg#0: a force couple turns the loop
cards.13.svg#6: loop cross-section: × current in, • current out
cards.13.svg#7: the commutator reverses the current every half turn
cards.13.key: In a motor, the current and the magnetic field create a force. This force then turns the coil.
cards.13.etk.soru: Explore the parts of an electric motor.
cards.13.etk.noktalar.0.acik: This is the north pole of the magnet. The field lines leave from here.
cards.13.etk.noktalar.1.acik: This is the south pole of the magnet. The field lines enter here.
cards.13.etk.noktalar.2.acik: The field between the poles points from N to S.
cards.13.etk.noktalar.3.acik: Here you see the cross-section of the loop. The current flows in (×) on the left side and out (•) on the right side. Since the currents are opposite, the forces are opposite too.
cards.13.etk.noktalar.4.acik: A force of F = B·I·L acts on each side. The opposite forces on the two sides form a force couple.
cards.13.etk.noktalar.5.acik: The force couple turns the loop. The commutator reverses the current every half turn, and the rotation continues in the same direction.
cards.14.p:
• Like poles repel, opposite poles attract. There is no single pole.
• A current creates a field: B = 2k·I/d, B = 4πk·N·I/L.
• For parallel wires, F/L = 2k·I₁·I₂/d.
• The force is F = B·I·L·sinθ and F = q·v·B·sinθ.
• A charge entering perpendicular moves in a circle.
cards.14.svg#9: a charge entering ⊥ to B circles; no work is done
quiz.0.q: A long straight wire carries a current of 10 A. What is the magnetic field 5 cm from the wire in μT? (k = 10<sup>−7</sup> T·m/A)
quiz.0.e: B = 2k·I/d = 2·10<sup>−7</sup>·10/0.05 = 4·10<sup>−5</sup> T = 40 μT. If you forget to convert d to meters, you get a result 100 times too small.
quiz.1.q: A wire carrying current to the right in the plane of the page sits in a uniform magnetic field pointing into the page (⊗). In which direction is the force on the wire?
quiz.1.o.0: Up, in the plane of the page
quiz.1.o.1: Down, in the plane of the page
quiz.1.e: In the right-hand rule, the four fingers are held in the direction of B (into the page) and the thumb in the direction of I (to the right). In this case the palm faces up. The force is perpendicular to both I and B.
quiz.1.y.1: You found the opposite direction. Point your four fingers along B and your thumb along I. The palm shows the direction of the force.
quiz.1.y.2: The force must be perpendicular to the field. It cannot be in the same direction as the field.
quiz.1.y.3: The wire is perpendicular to the field (sinθ = 1). So the force is not zero. It is at its greatest.
quiz.2.q: Match each situation with its result.
quiz.2.ciftler.0.0: Parallel wires, currents in the same direction
quiz.2.ciftler.1.0: Parallel wires, currents in opposite directions
quiz.2.ciftler.2.0: Charge moving parallel to the field
quiz.2.ciftler.3.0: Charge entering perpendicular to the field
quiz.2.e: Parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract each other, and those carrying currents in opposite directions repel. A force of F = q·v·B·sinθ acts on a moving charge. For a charge moving parallel to the field, sinθ = 0. For a charge entering perpendicular to the field, the force is perpendicular to the velocity, so the charge moves in a circle.
quiz.3.q: An electron entering perpendicular to the field moves in a circle of radius r. If the magnetic field is doubled while its speed stays the same, what happens to the radius and the period?
quiz.3.e: r = m·v/(q·B) and T = 2πm/(q·B). Both are inversely proportional to B. So when B doubles, both are halved.
quiz.3.y.0: The period T = 2πm/(q·B) also depends on B. When B increases, the period gets shorter.
quiz.3.y.1: Since r = m·v/(q·B), when B grows the radius does not grow. It shrinks.
quiz.3.y.3: Since the force q·v·B grows, the path bends more. So the radius changes.
A:ozet: Push and pull magnets, then break one. Explore the field with a compass and look around a current-carrying wire. Build an electromagnet and measure the force on a wire.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Every magnet has an N (north) and an S (south) pole. Right now two N poles face each other. Flip the magnet on the right.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: Opposite poles attract each other, and like poles repel. Repulsion proves that an object is a magnet. Attraction is not proof, because a magnet also attracts an iron nail.
A:adimlar.1.metin: The left half of the bar magnet is the S pole and the right half is the N pole. What happens if you break it right in the middle?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: What happens to the pieces when a magnet is broken in the middle?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: One is only N, the other only S
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Poles cannot be separated from each other. A new pole forms at the broken end of each piece.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Magnetism comes from tiny magnets at the atomic scale. Breaking the magnet does not destroy them.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: New poles form at the broken ends right away. The right end of the left piece becomes N, and the left end of the right piece becomes S.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Move the compass to the numbered spots and watch how the needle turns.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: Where is the magnetic field strongest?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The lines gather and get denser at the poles. The field (B) is strongest there.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The lines are sparse in the middle region. So at spot 2 the field is only of medium strength.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Sparse lines mean a weak field. The field is weak at spots 1 and 6.
A:adimlar.3.metin: This is Oersted's experiment, and the wire is perpendicular to the screen. In the right-hand rule, the thumb shows the direction of the current and the curled fingers show the direction of the field. Turn on the current, reverse its direction, and look at the compasses.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: If the current goes into the screen (⊗), which way do the field lines circle?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: That happens when the current flows toward you (⊙). When the current reverses, the field reverses too.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: By the right-hand rule, the thumb shows the direction of the current (into the screen). The curled fingers then turn clockwise.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The field lines of a wire are circles around the wire. The compasses sit tangent to these circles.
A:adimlar.4.metin: A current of 2 A flows through the coil. Build an electromagnet that picks up exactly 8 paper clips.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: 40 turns with an iron core picked up 8 paper clips. The core itself becomes magnetized in the field of the coil and adds to the field.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.ipucu: A coil without a core is weak. First insert the iron core, then adjust the number of turns.
A:adimlar.5.metin: A force of F = B·I·L·sinθ acts on a current-carrying wire in a field. Here B = 0.2 T, I = 5 A, and L = 0.5 m. Adjust the angle so that the force is 0.25 N.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: F = 0.2 · 5 · 0.5 · sin30° = 0.5 · 0.5 = 0.25 N. The force is greatest when the wire is perpendicular to the field (0.5 N). When the wire is parallel to the field, the force is zero.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.ipucu: 0.2 · 5 · 0.5 makes 0.5 N. So sinθ must be 0.5.
A:adimlar.6.metin: The commutator is the part that reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn. This motor has no commutator, and the current always flows in the same direction.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: What would the coil do without a commutator?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: When the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the field, the forces on the sides lie along the same line and the torque is zero. The coil swings back and forth around this position.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Once the plane of the loop passes the position perpendicular to the field, the forces pull the coil back. For continuous rotation, the direction of the current has to be reversed.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: At the start the forces create a torque and the coil begins to turn. But the coil cannot turn continuously.
A:kapanis.0: Like poles repel each other, and opposite poles attract. Repulsion proves that an object is a magnet. There is no magnet with a single pole.
A:kapanis.1: Field lines run from N to S outside the magnet. Where the lines are dense, the field is strong. The N end of a compass shows the direction of the field.
A:kapanis.2: A wire carrying current creates a field around itself: B = 2k·I/d. The direction of the field is found with the right-hand rule.
A:kapanis.3: An electromagnet gets stronger with turns, current, and an iron core.
A:kapanis.4: A force of F = B·I·L·sinθ acts on a wire in a field. Thanks to the commutator, a motor turns this force into continuous rotation.
